lead: Scalability is the headroom a design leaves for growth. Elasticity is renting that headroom automatically for the minutes you need it and returning it after. A shop that keeps 18 servers all month pays for idle machines; an elastic shop runs one server at night and eighteen during a four-hour rush. Cloud systems use this to survive cricket-final spikes and local power cuts without over-buying. The same ideas choose load balancers, replica counts and auto-scaling rules.
prereq: You need: 6.4 for service models, Unit 1 for speedup and load balancing, and Unit 5 for replication consistency models.

blocks.text: Vertical scaling replaces a machine with a bigger one: more cores, more RAM, a faster disk. It needs no program change, but it stops at the largest machine a provider sells and often costs more per unit of work. Horizontal scaling adds more machines and spreads work across them. It has no single-machine ceiling, but the program must run as several copies.

The limit on horizontal scaling is the serial part. If a fraction s of the work cannot be split, N workers give the speedup below. S(N) is speedup over one worker, s is the serial fraction from 0 to 1, and N is the number of workers. As N grows, S(N) tends to 1/s; with s=0.2 the ceiling is 5×, or 500 requests per second (req/s) if one server does 100.

blocks.where: S(N) is speedup, s is the serial fraction (0 ≤ s ≤ 1), and N is the number of servers.

blocks.text: A tier that keeps no user data in its own memory is stateless and scales out by adding copies behind a load balancer. A tier that keeps session state, uploaded files or a shopping cart in local memory is stateful; adding a copy splits users across machines that do not know each other. Move session state to a shared store or a signed cookie before scaling out.

Put a load balancer in front of identical servers. Round robin gives request 1 to server 1, request 2 to server 2, and so on; it assumes equal request cost. Weighted round robin gives a stronger server more turns. Least connections picks the server with the fewest open requests, which suits long-lived connections. IP hash uses hash(client IP) mod N and pins a client to one server; it breaks when N changes. Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring, so adding one server moves only its share of keys, not all keys. That gives cache affinity without rehashing everything.
Health checks probe each server; a failed probe removes it from the pool. Sticky sessions keep one user on one server, but they make failures and scaling harder. Prefer a shared session store.

Replication keeps copies for read scale and failure. In primary-replica, writes go to the primary and reads to replicas. A multi-primary setup accepts writes at more than one node, but conflict reconciliation becomes the hard part. With N replicas, a write must reach W replicas and a read contacts R replicas. If R+W>N, the read set and write set overlap, so the read sees the latest write. For N=3, W=2, R=2: 4>3. Read replicas scale reads, not writes.
Sharding splits data by key, for example a user-ID range, so each shard is small. Cross-shard queries and transactions become the cost; see 6.3.

Elasticity is automatic scaling: a controller watches a metric, compares it with a threshold, and changes the server count. CPU utilisation is common. Queue length and requests per second are better when work arrives in bursts. A cool-down waits after a scaling action so the metric settles; without it the controller adds servers, sees CPU fall, removes them, and thrashes.

Reactive auto-scaling responds to current load. Scheduled scaling adds servers before a known peak, such as 8 p.m. match time. Predictive scaling learns the daily pattern and acts earlier. All three need a maximum and minimum count, because a runaway rule can create a large bill.

Monitoring uses three streams: metrics are numbers over time, logs are events, traces follow one request across services. An SLI is a measured indicator, for example successful requests ÷ total requests. An SLO is the target for that SLI. An SLA is the contract with penalties. Availability of 99.9% leaves 0.1% downtime; in a 30-day month of 720 h that is 0.001×720×60 = 43.2 minutes. Over-provisioning buys safety with idle hours; the worked example prices it.

figure.caption: With 16 servers the ideal line reaches 1,600 req/s, but a 20% serial part flattens at 400 req/s. Notice that more servers cannot remove the serial work.

spec.aria: A plot of throughput against number of servers: the straight line is perfect scaling at 100 requests per second per server, and the flattening curve is the same system with a 20 percent serial part, reaching only 400 at 16 servers.

examples.question: An app must serve 2,000 requests per second at peak. Each request needs 50 ms of CPU on one core, and a server has 8 cores. You size servers to run at 70% utilisation. The app needs 1 server off peak and full capacity for 4 hours a day, 30 days a month, at ₹6 per server-hour. (a) How many servers at peak? (b) What does elastic scaling cost per month? (c) What would 18 fixed servers cost, and how much does elasticity save?
steps: One core serves 1 ÷ 0.050 s = 20 requests per second (req/s).
At 70% utilisation, usable capacity is 0.70 × 160 = 112 req/s.
Peak hours = 4 h/day × 30 days = 120 h. Total hours = 30 × 24 = 720 h. Off-peak = 720 − 120 = 600 h.
examples.answer: Peak needs 18 servers; elastic cost is ₹16,560 per month; 18 fixed servers cost ₹77,760, so elasticity saves ₹61,200.
examples.check:
import math
peak_rps = 2000
cpu_per_req = 0.050
cores = 8
utilisation = 0.70
per_core = 1 / cpu_per_req
per_server = per_core * cores
usable = per_server * utilisation
servers = math.ceil(peak_rps / usable)
peak_hours = 4 * 30
total_hours = 30 * 24
off_peak_hours = total_hours - peak_hours
rate = 6
cost_elastic = off_peak_hours * 1 * rate + peak_hours * servers * rate
cost_fixed = total_hours * servers * rate
saving = cost_fixed - cost_elastic
print(servers)
print(int(usable))
print(cost_elastic)
print(cost_fixed)
print(saving)

traps: Scalability and elasticity are not synonyms: scalability is possible growth, elasticity is automatic and timed growth.
Scaling out a server that keeps the session in local memory splits users across machines that cannot see each other's sessions.
Amdahl's law says adding servers cannot remove the serial part; speedup saturates at 1/s, not at N.
The quorum rule is R+W>N, not R+W≥N; equality can leave a read set and a write set disjoint.
Auto-scaling on CPU alone with no cool-down can thrash: add, remove, add, remove.

quiz.q: Define scalability and elasticity in one sentence each.
quiz.a: Scalability is the ability of a design to handle growth; elasticity is automatic addition and removal of resources to match demand.

quiz.q: Why does a stateless tier scale out more easily than a stateful tier?
quiz.a: Any server can handle any request, so a load balancer can add or remove copies without moving a user's session.

quiz.q: N=5 replicas, W=3. What is the smallest R that satisfies R+W>N?
quiz.a: R+3>5, so R>2; smallest integer R=3.

quiz.q: A job has s=0.10. Find speedup at N=10 and the ceiling as N→∞.
Peak load is 1,500 req/s. Each request uses 40 ms of CPU on one core, a server has 4 cores, and you run at 75% utilisation. How many servers?
quiz.a: One core: 1/0.040=25 req/s; server: 4×25=100; usable: 0.75×100=75; servers=ceil(1500/75)=20.

quiz.q: Why does an auto-scaler need a cool-down?
quiz.a: To let a scaling action affect the metric before the next decision, which prevents rapid add-remove thrashing.

quiz.q: An SLA promises 99.95% availability for a 30-day month. How many minutes of downtime does it allow?
What are SLI, SLO and SLA?
quiz.a: SLI is a measured service indicator; SLO is the target for it; SLA is the contract with penalties.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems often use Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or cloud auto-scaling groups, with queue-length metrics and predictive rules. Serverless functions push elasticity to per-request scaling. Research looks at cost-aware auto-scaling and carbon-aware scheduling. Search for “horizontal pod autoscaler”, “quorum reads and writes” and “SLO error budget”.
